content: Men who have sex with men (MSM) were asked to complete a self-administered questionnaire distributed through gay venues and community websites. Among 443 HIV-negative respondents, 40% expressed interest in participating in a future on-demand pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) trial. Factors independently associated with this interest included lower educational levels, having more than 20 male sexual partners in the previous year, engaging in unprotected anal sex with casual partners, and preferring PrEP follow-up visits in a dedicated area within a hospital. Confidentiality and tailored counseling during PrEP follow-up were identified as critical issues. A study conducted in two U.S. HIV epicenters examined MSM's knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding daily PrEP use. Multivariable logistic regression analysis revealed that drug use and sexual risk behaviors were associated with willingness to take PrEP. Awareness and use of PrEP were low, highlighting the need for innovative strategies to educate MSM about this prevention method. Future studies should explore how non-injection drug use may impact PrEP adherence. Another study focused on high-risk, substance-using MSM in Boston, Massachusetts, explored the influence of sexual relationships on PrEP use. MSM generally viewed main partners as supportive of PrEP use, while disclosure to casual partners was deemed unnecessary due to the informal nature of these relationships. HIV-related stigma and substance use were barriers to discussing PrEP with casual partners. Behavioral interventions to improve PrEP adherence should be tailored to the type of sexual partnership. Substance-using, high-risk MSM expressed a preference for daily PrEP dosing over intermittent use. Reasons included ease of integration into daily routines, concerns about missing doses due to drug or alcohol use, privacy concerns, reluctance to carry pills outside the home, and difficulty planning ahead for sexual activity. Daily dosing may enhance adherence and acceptability of PrEP in this population. In Peru, MSM and transgender women (TGW) reported high acceptability of both oral and rectal PrEP, particularly among those at the highest risk of HIV infection. These findings can guide the implementation of PrEP programs in similar settings and populations. A nationwide study in France assessed awareness and discussion of PrEP among individuals with HIV. While a significant number were aware of PrEP, sharing antiretroviral drugs for PrEP with HIV-negative individuals was not common. Discussions about PrEP were more frequent among those with HIV-negative partners. These findings suggest that individuals with HIV are not widely sharing their medications for PrEP use. In New York City, an online sample of young MSM revealed low prior knowledge of PrEP, with only 7% having heard of it. However, 35% expressed interest in PrEP after learning about its efficacy. HIV knowledge and risk behaviors, rather than demographics, were significant predictors of PrEP interest. More education and research are needed to inform PrEP uptake strategies. A study in San Francisco examined male couples' awareness and attitudes toward PrEP. While 62% had heard of PrEP, many confused it with post-exposure prophylaxis. Concerns about risk compensation and uncertainty about healthcare providers offering PrEP to anyone requesting it were common. Those at greatest risk were less receptive to PrEP, while those at moderate risk showed more interest. These findings underscore the need for targeted education and identification of populations where PrEP can have the highest impact. In Thailand, a study among MSM in the iPrEx trial identified facilitators and barriers to medication adherence. Factors such as social support, healthcare access, and substance use influenced adherence. Tailored interventions are necessary to address these barriers and improve PrEP utilization in this population.
